extraction.name: Visual Question Answering (VQA)
extraction.description: A review of visual question answering datasets, algorithms, evaluation metrics, and future challenges. It discusses the limitations of existing VQA benchmarks and summarizes major datasets released since 2014.
extraction.creator: Kushal Ka and Christopher Kanan
extraction.rai:dataCollection: DAQUAR consists of QA pairs based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 dataset; additional ground truth answers were collected for DAQUAR to create DAQUAR-consensus. The section does not describe the original collection procedure in detail.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images from the NYU-DepthV2 dataset, with QA pairs derived from those images.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: COCO-VQA used Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to generate questions by being asked to "Stump a smart robot," and a separate pool of workers generated the answers; each question was then answered by 10 independent annotators. Visual Genome used two collection modes: free-form questions and region-specific prompting about image regions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is about 83.3%; the paper also discusses consensus-based evaluation and notes that DAQUAR-consensus collected an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: COCO-VQA: 10 answers per question; DAQUAR-consensus: average of 5 ground truth answers per question
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: An NLP algorithm was used to derive COCO-QA question-answer pairs from COCO image captions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper identifies strong language bias and dataset bias in VQA benchmarks: questions often constrain answers, question wording strongly affects predictions, and models can rely more on language than image content. It also notes that answer distributions are unbalanced (e.g., 'yes' more common than 'no').
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Existing VQA datasets and benchmarks are limited by bias, evaluation inconsistencies, and insufficient coverage of harder question types. The paper says current benchmarks are not sufficient to evaluate whether VQA is solved, and that open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation each have shortcomings. It also recommends that systems should not rely solely on binary questions or answer choices provided as inputs.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper mentions real-world VQA applications such as enabling blind users to ask questions about visual content, and argues that biased datasets limit deployment and real-world utility. It also frames VQA as relevant to a visual Turing test and broader AI progress.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The datasets are discussed as benchmarks for training and evaluation/testing of VQA algorithms, including open-ended and multiple-choice evaluation. The paper recommends using mean per-question-type performance and carefully selected multiple-choice options, and says future datasets should be larger and less biased.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For COCO-VQA, multiple answers per question were collected and used in a consensus-based evaluation metric; for Visual7W, plausible answers were collected by prompting annotators without seeing the image; for SYNTH-VQA, synthetic images were used to create a more varied and balanced dataset and reduce biases.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: COCO-QA questions were generated from COCO captions using an NLP algorithm that breaks longer sentences into smaller chunks; the dataset was constrained to four question types and single-word answers. Visual Genome used region-specific question prompting based on descriptive bounding-box annotations.

name.evidence: “Visual Question Answering (VQA) is a recent problem in computer vision and natural language processing...”

description.evidence: “In this review, we critically examine the current state of VQA in terms of problem formulation, existing datasets, evaluation metrics, and algorithms.”

inLanguage.evidence: The paper is written in English.

rai:dataCollection.evidence: “It consists of 6795 training and 5673 testing QA pairs based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset” and “additional ground truth answers were collected for DAQUAR to create an alternative evaluation metric.”

rai:dataCollectionType.evidence: “QA pairs based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset”

rai:dataCollectionRawData.evidence: “QA pairs based on images from the NYU-DepthV2 Dataset”

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: “Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image by being asked to `Stump a smart robot,' and a separate pool of workers were hired to generate the answers to the questions.” / “Each of the questions is then answered by 10 independent annotators.” / “Two distinct modes of data collection were used... In the free-form method, annotators were free to ask any question about an image... The creators of Visual Genome combated this by also prompting workers to ask questions about specific image regions.”

rai:dataAnnotationPlatform.evidence: “Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) workers were employed to generate questions for each image...”

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: “These complications are reflected by inter-human agreement on this dataset, which is about 83%.” / “Using Accuracy V QA, the inter-human agreement on COCO-VQA is only 83.3%.” / “For DAQUAR-consensus, an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected.”

rai:annotationsPerItem.evidence: “COCO-VQA consists of three questions per image, with ten answers per question.” / “For DAQUAR-consensus, an average of five human annotated ground truth answers per question were collected.”

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: “In COCO-QA [31], QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions.”

rai:dataBiases.evidence: “the datasets tend to have strong bias”; “language bias in datasets critically affects the performance of the current VQA systems”; “In COCO-VQA, ‘yes’ is a much more common answer than ‘no,’ simply because people tend to ask questions biased toward ‘yes’ as an answer.”

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: “Existing VQA benchmarks are not sufficient to evaluate whether an algorithm has ‘solved’ VQA.”; “A system that is solely capable of operating with answers provided is not really solving VQA, because these are not available when a system is deployed.”; “A VQA system should be capable of more than solely binary questions so that its abilities can be fully assessed.”

rai:dataSocialImpact.evidence: “All real-world applications for VQA, such as enabling the blind to ask questions about visual content, require the output of the VQA system to be open-ended.”; “Language bias in datasets critically affects the performance of the current VQA systems, which limits their deployment.”

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: “algorithms do not have enough data for training and evaluation”; “multiple-choice has been proposed as a way to evaluate VQA algorithms”; “mean per-question type performance should replace standard accuracy”; “Future datasets need to be larger”; “Future datasets need to be less biased.”

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: “Each of the questions is then answered by 10 independent annotators. The multiple answers per question are used in the consensus-based evaluation metric” and “Plausible answers are collected by prompting annotators to answer the question without seeing the image.” and “By using synthetic images, it becomes possible to create a more varied and balanced dataset. Natural image datasets tend to have more consistent context and biases... Using synthetic images, these biases can be reduced.”

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: “QA pairs are created for images using an Natural Language Processing (NLP) algorithm that derives them from the COCO image captions. Longer sentences are broken into smaller chunks for ease of processing” and “All of the questions have a single word answer” and “The creators of Visual Genome combated this by also prompting workers to ask questions about specific image regions. Region-specific question prompting was made possible using Visual Genome's descriptive bounding-box annotations.”
